---
title: "Fitting the He et al. (2010) seasonal SEIR to synthetic data"
subtitle: "What camdl's defaults get you, and how to read what they tell you"
execute:
  echo: true
  warning: false
---

This chapter fits the He et al. [-@he2010] seasonal SEIR measles model
to *synthetic* data generated from the published MLE. Synthetic
recovery is the cleanest possible test of an inference pipeline: we
know the answer, the data come from the same process the inference
assumes, and any failure to recover truth localizes to either a
modelling artifact or an inference artifact rather than to
model misspecification.

**Pedagogical principle.** Every numeric setting that *can* be a camdl
default *is* a camdl default in this chapter. Stage cooling, chain
count, particle count, iteration count — all camdl-shipped values.
The chapter's job is to show what those defaults do on a real
multimodal problem, how to read the diagnostics camdl emits, and how
to remediate when a default doesn't suffice. Fitting is rarely
push-button; learning to fit is mostly learning to read the failure
modes.

The chapter is structured around a single linear fit attempt. We
will not preview results before showing them, will not stage problems
to demonstrate features, and will not interpret point estimates
before checking convergence. When the compound gate fails — and on
this problem at default budget it likely will, on at least one of its
two legs — we treat the failure as the lesson and respond to it the
way a working analyst would.

> **An archived earlier draft of this chapter** ran on a buggier
> version of camdl (extraction-bias, looser scout gate,
> non-default cooling) and reached conclusions about identifiability
> ridges that turned out to be mostly real but partially confounded
> with pipeline artifacts. That draft is preserved at
> [`he2010-v0-synthetic`](he2010-v0-synthetic.qmd) for context. This
> chapter is the rewrite against camdl `ba334a9` and later (compound
> gate, clean-evaluation chain selection, atomic Â/`chain_agreement`
> rename in MLE outputs).

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
import os, sys, subprocess, tomllib, io
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# _lib path is absolute so it works regardless of quarto's cwd
_LIB = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "_lib" if "__file__" in dir() \
       else Path("/Users/vsb/projects/work/camdl-book/vignettes/_lib")
sys.path.insert(0, str(_LIB))
from pair_plot import pair_plot_chains, load_chain_traces

GREY = "#666666"
plt.rcParams.update({
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.labelcolor": GREY, "xtick.color": GREY, "ytick.color": GREY,
    "axes.edgecolor": GREY, "legend.edgecolor": GREY,
})

VDIR = Path("he2010")
MODEL  = VDIR / "models/he2010_london.camdl"
PARAMS = VDIR / "params/he2010_london.toml"
SYNTH  = VDIR / "data/he2010_synthetic_obs.tsv"
REAL   = VDIR / "data/he2010_london_cases.tsv"

# ── freshness check ────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Every chapter's opening cell asserts that downstream artifacts are
# at least as new as their upstream sources. If anything is stale,
# render fails loudly with the make target the reader needs to run.
def assert_fresh(path, *deps, hint=""):
    if not path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"{path} missing — {hint}")
    pm = path.stat().st_mtime
    for d in deps:
        if Path(d).stat().st_mtime > pm:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"{path} is older than {d}. Run: {hint}")
    return path

# Synthetic obs must be newer than model + truth params.
assert_fresh(SYNTH, MODEL, PARAMS, hint="cd vignettes/he2010 && make sim")

# Fit results — Round 1 (fit-*) and Round 2 (fit_r2-*) live in
# separate hashed dirs. Each round has its own scout / refine.
def _find_fit(prefix):
    # Only count a fit dir as present if its scout has fit_state.toml
    # (i.e. scout completed, not mid-run).
    hits = sorted((VDIR / "results/fits").glob(f"{prefix}/real/fit_42"))
    return next((h for h in reversed(hits)
                 if (h / "scout/fit_state.toml").exists()), None)

R1_ROOT = _find_fit("fit-*")
R2_ROOT = _find_fit("fit_r2-*")
if R1_ROOT is None:
    raise RuntimeError(
        "no Round 1 fit results in vignettes/he2010/results/fits/. "
        "Run: cd vignettes/he2010 && make fit-r1")
R1_SCOUT,  R1_REFINE  = R1_ROOT / "scout",  R1_ROOT / "refine"
R2_SCOUT  = (R2_ROOT / "scout")  if R2_ROOT else None
R2_REFINE = (R2_ROOT / "refine") if R2_ROOT else None
```

## 1. Forward-simulation validation

Before any inference work, we validate that camdl's chain-binomial
backend produces the same forward-simulation distribution at the He
et al. MLE as the pomp reference [@king2016pomp] for the same model.
Recovery experiments against a buggy simulator are meaningless —
"recovered to truth" tells us nothing if the truth-trajectory is
itself wrong.

The smoke test runs ~200 forward simulations at the He et al. MLE
under camdl, compares ensemble medians and IQR on total cases and
last-year cases against a pre-computed pomp ensemble, and exits
non-zero if any metric falls outside tolerance.

```{bash}
#| label: envelope-smoke
#| echo: true
cd vignettes/he2010 && python validation/envelope_smoke.py
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Camdl-pomp parity history (camdl#11)

An earlier version of this chapter (the `-v0` archive) discovered two
unit-conversion bugs in camdl by running this exact smoke test:
`iota` was being interpreted as a rate when it should have been a
dimensionless count floor, and `birthrate` was being divided by
365.25 twice. Both surfaced as catastrophic envelope mismatch
(0% epidemic persistence in camdl vs. 100% in pomp). Both were
fixed upstream in camdl#11. This kind of regression test is what
catches them.
:::

## 2. The synthetic dataset

We generate one synthetic dataset from the He et al. MLE at seed 42,
21 years of weekly notifications matching the real London time
series.

```{bash}
#| label: show-sim-command
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Already run by `make sim`; here is the command verbatim.
cd vignettes/he2010 && camdl simulate models/he2010_london.camdl \
    --params params/he2010_london.toml \
    --backend chain_binomial --dt 1 --seed 42 \
    --obs-only data/he2010_synthetic_obs.tsv
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-synth-vs-real
#| fig-cap: "Synthetic data (top) generated at the He et al. MLE under seed 42 vs. the real London notifications 1944–1964 (bottom). Visual similarity here is *not* the validation criterion — see the data-leakage callout below."
synth = pl.read_csv(SYNTH, separator="\t")
real  = pl.read_csv(REAL,  separator="\t")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 4.5), sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(synth["time"], synth["weekly_cases"], color="#3366cc", linewidth=0.8)
axes[0].set_ylabel("synth weekly cases")
axes[1].plot(real["time"], real["cases"], color="#222222", linewidth=0.8)
axes[1].set_ylabel("real weekly cases")
axes[1].set_xlabel("time (days from 1944-01-07)")
fig.tight_layout()
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Subtle and pernicious: cherry-picking synthetic seeds

A natural temptation in a recovery study is to *select* a synthetic
draw that "looks like" the real data — visually matching biennial
peak heights, troughs, between-year regularity. **Do not.** Once you
filter draws by features of the real data, the inference is no
longer a clean recovery test: you have leaked structure of the real
data into the supposedly-blind ground truth, and any "successful
recovery" reflects how well your filter encoded that structure
rather than how well the inference machinery works. Use the first
seed you draw, or pre-register a seed schedule. The pipeline either
recovers or it doesn't; the data realization is what it is.

This applies equally to *any* tuning informed by the truth dataset:
adjusting bounds based on where truth happens to sit, picking
cooling schedules that worked well on this seed, choosing
particle counts that gave clean diagnostics last time. All of it
leaks. The only escape is to commit to settings *before*
inspecting the recovery result.
:::

## 3. Fitting: a diagnostic-driven loop

Fitting is rarely push-button. The transferable knowledge in this
chapter isn't a particular budget that worked, it's the loop:

> Run a principled first attempt → read the compound gate → let the
> failing leg dictate the next scaling decision → repeat until the
> gate passes (or until the gate's persistent refusal becomes
> evidence of structural unidentifiability).

We illustrate one full turn of that loop here. Round 1 starts at
camdl's package defaults — the smallest budget at which the gate is
designed to be informative. Round 2 scales based on what Round 1's
gate says, not on a pre-decided budget.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why start at camdl defaults?

Camdl's stage defaults — 8 chains × 500 particles × 30 iterations
for scout, 4 chains × 1000 particles × 50 iterations for refine —
are sized for a *typical* problem: medium-dimensional parameter
space, ≲ 200 observations, well-identified likelihood. They are
deliberately *not* sized for hard problems like this one. See the
[Inference Specification](../reference/inference-spec.qmd) for the
package author's reasoning.

Starting at defaults is not a claim that defaults will work. It is
the smallest principled budget that lets us read what the compound
gate flags. The gate's two legs — chain agreement Â and clean-eval
decibans-spread Δ_dB — surface different failure modes (chains
haven't mixed; chains found different basins; chains pinned at
bounds; PF impoverishment). Seeing *which* leg fires on a default
run tells us what to scale up:

- Â high uniformly across params → more iterations
- Â high on a subset, others fine → narrower bounds on the
  unidentified subset, or more chains to span basins
- Δ_dB high with Â low → more chains, possibly wider bounds, or
  multimodality investigation via profile
- Both pass at default budget → unusual; either the problem is
  easy or the gate is being lenient (check σ_max in the threshold)

Round 2 below uses the diagnostic from Round 1 to choose how to
scale, not a pre-decided budget.
:::

### 3.1 Round 1: defaults

The Round-1 fit configuration is below in full. Stage budgets mirror
camdl's `scout.rs`/`refine.rs` package defaults verbatim; the only
domain knowledge is in the `[estimate]` and `[fixed]` blocks
(physical bounds and He et al. published values).

```{bash}
#| label: show-fit-config
#| echo: true
cat vignettes/he2010/fit.toml
```

```{bash}
#| label: show-fit-command
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Already run by `make fit-r1`; here is the command verbatim.
cd vignettes/he2010 && camdl fit run fit.toml --seed 42 --progress plain
```

### 3.2 Reading the compound gate after Round 1

Camdl's scout-to-refine handoff is gated by **two** convergence
criteria, both of which must pass [see the `chain_agreement` /
clean-evaluation entries in the
[Inference Specification](../reference/inference-spec.qmd)]:

1. **Per-parameter chain agreement Â** — Gelman–Rubin's split-Â
   computed on the per-iteration parameter-mean trajectory across
   chains, last half of iterations. Tests whether independent IF2
   optimizers agreed on *where* in parameter space they ended.
2. **Clean-evaluation decibans-spread Δ_dB** — high-particle PF
   re-evaluation (default 4000 particles × 8 replicates,
   logmeanexp-combined) of each chain's winning candidate, rendered
   as the spread (max − min) in decibans across chains. Tests
   whether the basins those chains found are equally good in
   likelihood units, with an SE-aware floor that prevents the gate
   from firing on noise.

The Â leg is necessary but not sufficient. All chains can agree
per-parameter and still sit in basins separated by tens of thousands
of decibans — a failure mode that the Δ_dB leg exists to catch.

```{python}
#| label: r1-scout-gate
#| echo: true
def report_gate(stage_path, label):
    if not (stage_path / "fit_state.toml").exists():
        print(f"{label}: not produced (upstream gate refused handoff).")
        return
    state = tomllib.loads((stage_path / "fit_state.toml").read_text())
    agreement = state.get("tail_chain_agreement", {})
    chain_lls = state.get("chain_clean_logliks", [])
    chain_ses = state.get("chain_clean_ses", [])
    print(f"{label}:")
    print(f"  {'param':<12} {'Â':>6}  status")
    for p, a in sorted(agreement.items()):
        flag = "✓" if a < 1.05 else ("~" if a < 1.10 else "✗")
        print(f"  {p:<12} {a:>6.3f}  {flag}")
    if chain_lls:
        nats_to_db = 10.0 / np.log(10)
        delta_db = (max(chain_lls) - min(chain_lls)) * nats_to_db
        sigma_max = max(chain_ses) if chain_ses else 0.0
        threshold_db = max(30.0, 8.0 * sigma_max * nats_to_db)
        flag = "✓" if delta_db < threshold_db else "✗"
        print(f"  Δ_dB = {delta_db:.1f} dB / threshold {threshold_db:.1f} dB "
              f"(σ_max={sigma_max:.2f} nats) {flag}")

report_gate(R1_SCOUT,  "Round 1 scout")
print()
report_gate(R1_REFINE, "Round 1 refine")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-r1-trajectories
#| fig-cap: "Round 1 scout: per-chain log-likelihood trajectories across 30 IF2 iterations. Raw in-run `if2_perturbed_loglik` at 500 particles (noisy, ~30-nat per-eval SD). Dashed line = truth ℓ ≈ −5983. Five chains dove into a bad basin during cooling iter 13–25 before partially recovering; three stayed in the better region throughout. Clean-eval at iter 30 pulled all chains back into a narrower cluster (see §3.2 verdict above) but best chain still ~252 nats below truth."
def load_traces(scout_dir):
    dfs = []
    chain_dirs = [p for p in scout_dir.glob("chain_*")
                  if p.is_dir() and p.name.split("_")[1].isdigit()]
    for cd in sorted(chain_dirs, key=lambda p: int(p.name.split("_")[1])):
        cid = int(cd.name.split("_")[1])
        lines = [l for l in (cd/"parameter_traces.tsv").read_text().splitlines()
                 if not l.startswith("#")]
        df = pl.read_csv(io.StringIO("\n".join(lines)), separator="\t",
                         infer_schema_length=10000)
        dfs.append(df.with_columns(pl.lit(cid).alias("chain")))
    return pl.concat(dfs)

import io
TRUTH_LL = -5982.7   # 16k-particle reference from v0 archive
t1 = load_traces(R1_SCOUT)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
for c in sorted(t1["chain"].unique()):
    sub = t1.filter(pl.col("chain") == c).sort("iteration")
    ax.plot(sub["iteration"], sub["if2_perturbed_loglik"],
            linewidth=1.1, alpha=0.85, label=f"chain {c}")
ax.axhline(TRUTH_LL, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1,
           label=f"truth ℓ = {TRUTH_LL:.1f}")
ax.set_xlabel("IF2 iteration"); ax.set_ylabel("log-likelihood (in-run, 500 particles)")
ax.set_title("Round 1 scout: per-chain ll trajectories")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7, ncol=1, loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5))
fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-r1-extraction-bias
#| fig-cap: "Round 1: in-run 500-particle PF log-likelihood at iter 30 (the value camdl's IF2 reports as `final_ll`) vs the clean-eval winner ll for each chain (4000p × 8 reps, logmeanexp). The 56-nat gap on chain 6 (in-run −6192 → clean-eval −6235) is selection-on-PF-noise: at 500p single-eval SD ≈ 30 nats, argmax over 8 chains accumulates ~σ√(2·ln 8) ≈ 60 nats of optimistic bias. This is the v0 extraction-bias pathology that camdl unit A's clean-eval was built to eliminate."
def chain_in_run_final(scout_dir):
    out = []
    for cd in sorted(scout_dir.glob("chain_*"),
                     key=lambda p: int(p.name.split("_")[1])
                     if p.is_dir() and p.name.split("_")[1].isdigit() else -1):
        if not cd.is_dir() or not cd.name.split("_")[1].isdigit():
            continue
        cid = int(cd.name.split("_")[1])
        df = pl.read_csv(io.StringIO(
            "\n".join(l for l in (cd/"parameter_traces.tsv").read_text().splitlines()
                      if not l.startswith("#"))),
            separator="\t", infer_schema_length=10000)
        df = df.with_columns(pl.col("loglik").cast(pl.Float64, strict=False))
        ll_finite = df.filter(pl.col("loglik").is_not_null())
        if ll_finite.height:
            out.append((cid, float(ll_finite.tail(1)["loglik"].item())))
    return out

inrun = chain_in_run_final(R1_SCOUT)
state1 = tomllib.loads((R1_SCOUT / "fit_state.toml").read_text())
clean_lls = state1.get("chain_clean_logliks", [])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for cid, ir in inrun:
    ce = clean_lls[cid - 1]
    ax.plot([cid, cid], [ir, ce], color="#888888", linewidth=1)
    ax.scatter(cid, ir, color="#3366cc", s=70, zorder=3,
               label="in-run final_ll (500p)" if cid == inrun[0][0] else None)
    ax.scatter(cid, ce, color="#cc3333", s=70, marker="s", zorder=3,
               label="clean-eval (4000p × 8)" if cid == inrun[0][0] else None)
ax.axhline(TRUTH_LL, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1,
           label=f"truth ℓ = {TRUTH_LL:.0f}")
ax.set_xlabel("chain"); ax.set_ylabel("log-likelihood")
ax.set_title("Round 1: in-run vs clean-eval ll per chain — extraction bias visible per chain")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5))
fig.tight_layout()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why we need clean-eval (and what it can and can't fix)

The traditional IF2 winner-selection pipeline picks the chain with
the highest in-run log-likelihood at the final iteration. That number
is an *unreliable* estimator of which chain actually ended up in the
best place, for two compounding reasons:

1. **PF noise is large at low particle counts.** At 500 particles
   on 1096 weekly observations, a single PF evaluation has SD
   ≈ 30 nats. With 8 chains and an argmax selection, the expected
   *upward* bias of the winning chain's reported ll is roughly
   $\sigma\sqrt{2\log N} \approx 60$ nats — pure selection on noise.
2. **The reported in-run `final_ll` evaluates the *particle cloud*,
   not the final parameter vector.** IF2's perturbations smear the
   cloud across parameter space, so the cloud average can score
   well even when the cloud's *mean* (the param vector you'd
   actually use downstream) is in a bad region. Chain 6 in
   fig-r1-extraction-bias shows this dramatically: cloud ll ≈ −6192
   at iter 30, param-mean ll ≈ −8577 at the same iter — a 2400-nat
   gap explained entirely by which estimator you ask.

**Clean-eval does three things to fix this**:

- **Higher particles** (default 4000): drops single-eval SD from
  ~30 nats to ~3 nats.
- **Multiple replicates** (default 8) combined via `logmeanexp`:
  unbiased on the likelihood scale, drops SE another √8.
- **Three candidate vectors per chain** — `final_iter` (the cloud
  mean at last iter), `tail_mean_last_k` (averaged over last K
  iters), and `best_in_run_iter` (the chain's best visited θ̂
  during its run). The chain's reported score is the **max** over
  these three candidates' clean-eval scores.

**Does a bad chain stay bad?** *Mostly*, with an important
qualification. The candidate set picks each chain's *best visited
point*, not an invented one. If a chain spent its whole life in
a basin 2000 nats below truth, all three candidates score there
(`best_in_run_iter`'s "best" is still bad), and clean-eval
correctly reports a chain that's 2000 nats below truth. Chain 1
in R1 is exactly this case: final_iter −8422, best_in_run_iter
−8440 — no rescue, transparently bad.

**The qualification: `best_in_run_iter` reports a chain's best
*visited* point, not its *destination*.** If a chain transited a
good region during cooling and then drifted away, clean-eval
headlines the visit even if the chain ended in a bad basin. R1's
winner — chain 6 at ll=−6235 — is exactly this: chain 6's
final_iter scored −8400, but it briefly visited a region scoring
−6235 mid-run, and that's what's reported (see fig-r1-candidates
below). So the headline "best chain at −6235" is true at the level
of "this θ̂ vector exists in chain 6's history", but misleading if
read as "chain 6 converged to a good place".

This is why **the compound gate has two legs, not one**:

- **Â on the parameter trajectory** sees the *destination* and the
  iter-by-iter path. Chain 6's R₀ ended at ~88 with chains 5/7/8
  at ~60–90 in *different* basins → Â(R₀) = 1.21, fails. The
  trajectory diagnostic catches what `best_in_run_iter` hides.
- **Δ_dB across chain best-moments** still catches the
  multimodality independently. Chain 1's *best ever* point is at
  −8440; chain 6's at −6235; spread = 9500 dB. The chains didn't
  all transit the same good region.

A pipeline that reported only `best_in_run_iter` scores without the
Â trajectory check could plausibly launder a "chain 6 winner at
−6235" into a refine starting point and produce a "converged" MLE
that no Bayesian sanity check would survive. The gate refuses
exactly that handoff.

The deeper design point: `best_in_run_iter` is the right *warm-start
candidate* for refine (refine wants the best θ̂ regardless of where
the chain ended), but it is *not* a sufficient summary of "did this
chain converge". Refine starting from chain 6's good-visit θ̂ is
fine if Â on the broader cohort says chains agree. If Â says they
don't, the gate refuses regardless of how good the best-visited
point looks.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-r1-candidates
#| fig-cap: "Round 1: clean-eval log-likelihood of all three candidates per chain — `final_iter` (where the chain ended), `tail_mean_last_k` (averaged over last 50% of iters), and `best_in_run_iter` (best θ̂ visited during run). The chain's reported headline score is the max over its three candidates. Chain 6's headline winner ll = −6235 comes from its `best_in_run_iter` candidate; its `final_iter` candidate scores −8400 — chain 6 *visited* a good region during cooling but ended in a bad basin. Chains 1, 4 have all three candidates in the bad cluster (no transient visit, transparent failure). The gap between a chain's best candidate and its `final_iter` candidate is the 'rescue' magnitude: chains 2, 3, 6 had ~2000-nat rescues; chain 1 essentially zero. The Â trajectory leg of the gate catches what these single-point candidates can hide."
ce = pl.read_csv(io.StringIO(
    "\n".join(l for l in (R1_SCOUT/"chain_evaluations.tsv").read_text().splitlines()
              if not l.startswith("#"))),
    separator="\t", infer_schema_length=10000)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5))
markers = {"final_iter": ("o", "#3366cc", "final_iter (chain endpoint)"),
           "tail_mean_last_k": ("^", "#888888", "tail_mean_last_k"),
           "best_in_run_iter": ("s", "#cc3333", "best_in_run_iter (winner)")}
for cand, (mk, col, lbl) in markers.items():
    sub = ce.filter(pl.col("candidate") == cand)
    ax.scatter(sub["chain"], sub["loglik"], marker=mk, color=col, s=80,
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8, label=lbl, zorder=3)
ax.axhline(TRUTH_LL, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1,
           label=f"truth ℓ = {TRUTH_LL:.0f}")
ax.set_xlabel("chain"); ax.set_ylabel("clean-eval log-likelihood")
ax.set_title("Round 1: 3 clean-eval candidates per chain — visualizes the 'rescue' effect")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5))
ax.set_ylim(-12000, -5500)
fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-r1-ridge
#| fig-cap: "Round 1: final-iter (R₀, α) chain endpoints. Two clusters separated along the FOI ridge axis: a 'good basin' cluster (chains 5, 7, 8) at R₀ ≈ 60–90 with α ≈ 0.65–0.7, and a 'pinned-s₀' cluster (chains 1, 2, 3, 4, 6) where s₀ has saturated at the upper bound (0.95) and chains compensate via R₀ ≳ 80, α ≳ 0.9. Truth (black ×) is at R₀=56.8, α=0.976. With only 8 chains the two basins look discrete; the smoother ridge shape only becomes visible with more chains (see fig-r2-ridge)."
t1_final = (t1.group_by("chain")
              .agg(pl.col("iteration").max().alias("max_iter")))
final1 = t1.join(t1_final,
                 left_on=["chain", "iteration"],
                 right_on=["chain", "max_iter"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
ax.scatter(final1["R0"], final1["alpha"], c=final1["s0"],
           cmap="viridis", s=80, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8,
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-r1-chain-clean
#| fig-cap: "Round 1 clean-eval log-likelihood per chain (4000 particles × 8 replicates, logmeanexp combined). Error bars = clean-eval SE. Horizontal line = truth. Two distinct clusters clearly separated by ~2100 nats — the Δ_dB leg of the gate fires on exactly this spread (~9500 dB vs 30 dB threshold)."
state = tomllib.loads((R1_SCOUT / "fit_state.toml").read_text())
ll = state.get("chain_clean_logliks", [])
se = state.get("chain_clean_ses", [])
if ll:
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
    x = np.arange(1, len(ll)+1)
    ax.errorbar(x, ll, yerr=se, fmt="o", color="#3366cc",
                markersize=8, capsize=3, linewidth=1)
    ax.axhline(TRUTH_LL, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1,
               label=f"truth ℓ = {TRUTH_LL:.1f}")
    ax.set_xlabel("chain"); ax.set_ylabel("clean-eval log-likelihood")
    ax.set_title(f"R1 clean-eval: spread = {max(ll)-min(ll):.0f} nats "
                 f"≈ {(max(ll)-min(ll))*10/np.log(10):.0f} dB")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9,
              loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.5))
    fig.tight_layout()
```

**Reading the verdict.** Round 1 scout completed in ~80 s of IF2 +
~13 min of clean-eval, and the gate fired hard on both legs:

- **Â non-uniform**: alpha (1.61 ✗) and R₀ (1.21 ✗) failed the gate;
  the other four parameters passed. The pattern matters — chains
  agreed on (γ, σ, amplitude, s₀) but not on (R₀, α). This localizes
  the disagreement to the (R₀, α) sub-space, which is structurally
  the FOI ridge $\beta(t) (I+\iota)^\alpha$ sees in §5.
- **Δ_dB catastrophic**: chain clean-evaluated log-likelihoods span
  from −8423 to −6235, a spread of 2189 nats ≈ 9510 dB. The gate's
  threshold is 30 dB. This is a 350× breach — not "marginal
  multimodality," genuine basin disagreement.
- **Best chain log-lik = −6235.1 ± 2.2** at clean-eval. Truth is at
  ℓ ≈ −5983 (16k-particle reference). Even the best chain is
  **252 nats below truth** — Round 1 didn't even find the truth
  basin. Two distinct sub-optimal basins were sampled.
- **Refine refused.** The compound gate's whole purpose is exactly
  this refusal: scout output that hasn't agreed on a basin is not
  a starting point for refine. The error message points the user at
  three remediations: more chains/iterations, narrower bounds, or
  marking weakly-identified params as `ivp = true`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Bonus diagnostic: extraction-bias visible in 56 nats

Chain 6's in-run `final_ll = −6191.8` (camdl's per-chain printout,
500-particle PF eval at iter 30) versus its clean-eval winner
`−6235.1 ± 2.2` (4000 particles × 8 replicates, logmeanexp). The
56-nat difference is exactly the extraction-bias the camdl
clean-evaluation pass exists to correct: in-run 500-particle eval
has ~30-nat single-eval SD on this problem, and the
selection-on-noise bias when picking "best chain" by argmax over
in-run scores accumulates roughly $\sigma\sqrt{2 \log N}$ — for
σ ≈ 30 nats and N = 8 chains, that's ~60 nats. Chain 6 happened to
draw a favorable in-run noise sample at iter 30; clean-eval reveals
its true ll is closer to the bottom of the better basin's cluster.
This bias was the load-bearing pipeline issue in v0; the
remediation is shipped upstream in camdl `ba334a9`.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Bonus diagnostic: logit-transform compression

Camdl flagged two transform-position warnings:

```
amplitude  logit position |z|=3.8 — effective perturbation reduced
s0         logit position |z|=3.1 — effective perturbation reduced
```

The default logit transform on `amplitude ∈ [0.0001, 0.9999]` and
`s0 ∈ [0.001, 0.95]` puts the start values (0.4 and 0.05
respectively) far from the transformed-space midpoint 0. In logit
coordinates, perturbation of magnitude δ moves the parameter by
$\delta\,\sigma'(z)$ where $\sigma'$ is the logistic derivative —
which goes to zero at the bound corners. Chains starting near
those corners explore poorly. Camdl suggests `log` over `logit`
for compressed bounds; we leave that as a Round-3-or-later
investigation if Round 2's larger budget doesn't paper over it.
:::

### 3.3 Round 2: scaling from the diagnostic

Round 1's verdict was "Â high non-uniformly on (R₀, α) plus Δ_dB
catastrophically high." Per the §3 callout's rule table: more chains
(to span basins), more iterations (to let chains mix once they're in
a basin), and bumping particles is justified because 500 particles
on 1096 obs gives ~30 nat per-eval SD which makes the in-run trace
hard to read. None of these scaling decisions inspect the truth value
of any parameter — they're informed by the gate's two flags and by
problem features (data length, parameter dim) visible from the paper.

The Round-2 config is below; the diff from `fit.toml` is the
teaching artifact:

```{bash}
#| label: show-r2-config-diff
#| echo: true
diff vignettes/he2010/fit.toml vignettes/he2010/fit-r2.toml | head -40
```

```{bash}
#| label: show-r2-command
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Already run by `make fit-r2`; here is the command verbatim.
cd vignettes/he2010 && camdl fit run fit-r2.toml --seed 42 --progress plain
```

Total scout work: 16 × 100 × 2000 = 3.2M particle-iter units, ~27×
Round 1, ~4.5× *less* than the v0 archive's over-tuned 14.4M. The
budget choice is justified by the gate diagnosis, not by
foreknowledge of how much compute the answer needs.

**Reading the R2 verdict.** The figures tell a coherent story:

- **fig-r2-trajectories**: chains consolidate into a single cluster
  after ~iter 40. Three chains transiently visit a disaster region
  (ll ≪ −30,000) during mid-cooling but recover. The trajectories
  are much cleaner than R1's bimodal split.
- **fig-r2-chain-clean**: all 16 chains clean-evaluate to a single
  basin at ℓ ≈ −6286 to −6388 — spread 101 nats (~440 dB, still
  above the 30 dB threshold but ~200× tighter than R1's 9500 dB).
  The gate's Δ_dB failure is now *within-basin spread*, not
  *between-basin disagreement*.
- **fig-r2-ridge**: the 16 endpoints scatter by ~25 units in R₀ and
  ~0.05 in α; truth sits at the edge of the cloud, not at its
  centroid. Chains are wandering on a ridge in (R₀, α), not on a
  mixing-defect around a shared optimum.

**Verdict**: R2 converted R1's "multiple basins + extraction noise"
into "one consistent sub-optimal basin + residual (R₀, α) ridge
spread." The 300-nat gap to truth persists through tripled iterations,
doubled chains, and quadrupled particles. Adding compute has **reached
diminishing returns** for recovering truth on this parametrization —
the remaining signal says the data doesn't identify the (R₀, α)
combination at this resolution. The honest diagnostic move is §5
(profile likelihood), not Round 3.

::: {.callout-note}
## Stopping rule

If Round 2 passes the gate, we move to §4 (sampling-distribution
characterization). If Round 2 still fails, the chapter doesn't
silently spin up Round 3 — persistent gate failure after a principled
scale-up is itself evidence about the problem (likely structural
unidentifiability, which §5's profile likelihood is designed to
investigate). The loop terminates honestly, not with a budget that
finally launders the failure.
:::

## 4. Sampling variability of the MLE

A deeper question than "did this one fit recover truth" is "what is
the *sampling distribution* of the MLE at this DGP?" Even with a
bug-free pipeline running on a well-identified model, fitting one
realization of a stochastic DGP gives one MLE — different realizations
give different MLEs, and the spread of those MLEs is a property of
the data-generating process, not of the inference machinery.

This section runs the scout + refine pipeline on N independent
synthetic realizations (seeds 1..N) drawn from the same truth, and
reports the empirical distribution of recovered parameter estimates.

<!-- TODO: this is the chapter's anchor experiment. Implement once
the single-seed fit at default budget converges (or once we have

Concrete output: a (R₀, γ) scatter with truth marked, plus a table
of (param, mean estimate, sd, 95% CI, fraction of fits that passed
the gate). The take-home number is "X% of seeds at default budget
passed the gate; among those that did, the MLE has sampling SD ≈ Y
on R₀ and Z on γ." -->

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this section, and why nobody else does it

Most published synthetic-recovery studies show one realization. That
makes "the MLE was 5% off truth" hard to interpret: is 5% bias
indicative of a problem with the inference, or one-σ sampling
variability of an honest estimator? Without a sampling distribution
we can't tell. The 20-seed cloud here is what makes the chapter's
later claims about identifiability ridges defensible: bias along a
ridge axis should be much wider than bias across it, and the cloud
shape in (parameter, parameter) projections shows that directly.
:::

## 5. Identifiability analysis

For the He et al. parameterisation, the force of infection is

$$\lambda(t) \;=\; \beta(t)\,\frac{(I + \iota)^\alpha}{N},$$

where $\beta(t) = R_0 (\gamma + \mu)$ is the seasonally-modulated
contact rate and $\alpha$ is the mixing exponent. This form induces
an analytical ridge in $(s_0, \alpha)$: the early-epidemic infection
flux scales as $s_0 (i_0 + \iota)^\alpha$, so a perturbation that
increases $s_0$ by $\delta$ and decreases $\alpha$ by $\delta /
\log(i_0 + \iota)$ produces an identical flux to first order — a
direction in parameter space along which the likelihood is flat
[@he2010, Section 4.2 discusses this phenomenologically; the
derivation is in the v0 archive of this chapter].

<!-- TODO: lift the analytical derivation from the v0 archive
once the §3 fit lands. The ridge analysis is structural to the
problem and survives the pipeline cleanup; only the framing
("the data cannot identify one direction in 6D parameter space")
changes from v0's "why is the MLE biased?" -->

### Profile likelihood on s₀

The profile likelihood is the likelihood at each candidate $s_0$
value with the other parameters re-optimised — the honest
test of whether $s_0$ is identified by the data. We use camdl's
`profile` command, with IF2 starts at the scout MLE (not at truth —
that would leak) and re-optimization at each grid point.

<!-- TODO: profile_s0 cell, at modest grid (~16 points) and modest
particle count. Display the profile, mark scout MLE and truth s_0,
report the 1-nat and 2-nat intervals. -->

## 6. Fixed-s₀ fit

If §5's profile shows $s_0$ is poorly identified, fixing it at the
profile peak and re-fitting the remaining 5 parameters is the
canonical response: trade an unconstrained-but-undeterminable
parameter for a constrained-and-determinable conditional MLE. We
report the constraint cost (likelihood gap to the unconstrained
truth) and the residual bias on $(R_0, \gamma)$ to characterize
what the data does and does not tell us once the dominant ridge is
removed.

<!-- TODO: fixed-s0 fit, same defaults, report MLE table with
truth comparison + constraint-cost decomposition. -->

## What this chapter does not claim

A clean recovery on this problem at camdl-default budget would be
genuinely surprising. He et al. fit by maximum likelihood took
thousands of IF2 iterations across multiple bound-narrowing rounds;
the public MLE rests on calibration that no default could match. If
the chapter's §3 fit fails to recover truth within reasonable
sampling variability, the lesson is not that camdl is broken — it
is that *fitting is hard*, and that camdl's gate refused to launder
a non-converged scout into a refine output that would have looked
plausible per-parameter while masking basin-disagreement
internally. That refusal is the feature, not the failure mode.
